title: Confidentiality and information sharing
blurb: Protect what a woman tells you, let her control who is told, and share purposefully when safety demands it.
question: At a 16-week appointment, Priya tells her midwife that her partner hits her. She has a 2-year-old son and begs the midwife not to write anything in her notes because her partner reads them. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: A duty to protect and a duty to share
teach.body: Formally, a midwife owes a duty of confidentiality to all those receiving care, which includes making sure information about them is shared appropriately (Code 5). In plain English: what a woman tells you is hers. You share it with the people who need it to care for her and her baby, you tell her how it is used, and you share without her agreement only when safety and public protection override confidentiality.

head: Code
What it means on the ward
rows: Curtains, knock and wait, quiet voices at handover
Tell her who sees her notes and why
Applies after a maternal death or stillbirth
5.5 share with family as law allows
Partner and family on her terms
teach.caption: Caldicott principle 7: the duty to share for individual care is as important as the duty to protect confidentiality.

teach.body: A partner or mother is not entitled to her information because of the relationship. Involve the partner according to the woman's wishes (NG194 1.1.3). Give every woman at least one consultation without her partner, family member or guardian present (CG110 1.1.14), and ask about domestic abuse when she is alone (NG201 1.2.5). Use an independent interpreter, never her partner or family (CG110 1.3.10).

root.label: Information about a woman or baby

teach.caption: Children Act 2004 s16LA (in force 30 Sep 2026): sharing to safeguard a child does not breach confidence.

rows.label: Holds
values: Full record of care and test results

rows.label: Who may see it
values: Anyone at home who opens it

teach.caption: Tell her that what she discloses about abuse will be kept in a confidential record, not her hand-held notes.

teach.body: Midwife Jo hears Priya's disclosure. She thanks her, records it in the confidential record rather than the hand-held notes (CG110 1.5.8) and explains why and when information may need to be shared (CG110 1.1.9). Because a 2-year-old lives in the home, Jo shares the concern with children's social care under the safeguarding duty: consent is not required. She agrees a safe phone number with Priya and offers a domestic abuse support worker.

teach.caption: FGM Act 2003 s5B. The notification does not breach confidence.

teach.text: The s5B police duty covers girls UNDER 18. A woman of 18 or over with FGM needs a safeguarding assessment (risk to daughters or an unborn girl), not a mandatory police notification.

items: Code 5: privacy in all care, explain how information is used, confidentiality continues after death.
Partners and family are told what the woman agrees to; see her alone at least once.
Abuse disclosures go in a confidential record, not the hand-held notes.
Share without consent when safety overrides: children at risk (s16LA), FGM under 18 (s5B).
At transfer, pass on mental health, FGM, safeguarding and feeding information (NG194 1.1.8).

summary: You can now apply Code 5 to maternity care, keep the woman in control of who is told, and recognise when safety requires sharing without consent. You can also choose where sensitive disclosures are recorded and what to pass on at transfer of care.

A.q: On the postnatal ward, a woman's mother phones and asks whether her daughter needed a blood transfusion after the birth. The woman has not said what may be shared. What is the midwife's best response?
options: Explain that she cannot discuss the care and offer to pass on a message
Confirm the details, because the caller is the woman's next of kin
Give a brief summary of the birth without mentioning the transfusion
Ask the caller some security questions and then share the details
A.why: Information belongs to the woman. Without her agreement it is not shared with family, however close (Code 5.1, 5.5). Passing on a message keeps the caller connected without disclosure.

whyNot.1: Being next of kin gives no right to clinical information about an adult with capacity.
whyNot.2: Any summary of her birth is still confidential information shared without consent.
whyNot.3: Security questions confirm identity; they do not provide the woman's consent to disclosure.

A.q: According to the NMC Code, when should a midwife share necessary information with other professionals and agencies without the woman's agreement?
options: When her partner formally asks for it on her behalf
When the information is already written in her notes
When safety and public protection override confidentiality
When an outside agency puts its request in writing
A.why: Code 5.4: share necessary information only when the interests of patient safety and public protection override the need for confidentiality.

whyNot.0: A partner's request is not consent and does not create a safety override.
whyNot.1: Information already recorded is still confidential; its location does not change the test.
whyNot.3: A written request does not by itself justify disclosure; the safety and public protection test still applies.

A.q: Hana, 29, discloses domestic abuse at her booking appointment. She carries her hand-held notes everywhere. How should the midwife record the disclosure?
options: In the hand-held notes, so every professional sees it
In the baby's notes after the birth has taken place
In a confidential record, not in the hand-held notes
Not until she agrees to the police being informed
A.why: CG110 1.5.8: tell the woman the information will be kept in a confidential record and will not be included in her hand-held record, which her partner may read.

whyNot.0: Hand-held notes may be read at home by the abuser, putting her at greater risk.
whyNot.1: The disclosure concerns her now and must be recorded now, in the right place.
whyNot.3: Recording is part of safe care and does not depend on police involvement.

B.q: A community midwife is transferring care of a woman and her 12-day-old baby to the health visitor. Which item does NICE NG194 specifically list as information to share?
options: Her contraceptive history before pregnancy
Previous or current mental health concerns
The names of visitors during her inpatient stay
Her employer's details for maternity pay
B.why: NG194 1.1.8 lists previous or current mental health concerns, along with complications, FGM, safeguarding, parental responsibility, next of kin and feeding.

whyNot.0: Pre-pregnancy contraceptive history is not on the NG194 1.1.8 transfer list.
whyNot.2: Visitor names are not clinical information needed for ongoing care.
whyNot.3: Employment details are not part of the clinical handover NG194 describes.

B.q: Lena, 30, attends booking with her husband, who answers every question for her. Which action best protects her confidentiality and safety?
options: Ask every question with him present to build trust
Ask him to interpret her answers into English
Leave the domestic abuse question until 36 weeks
Arrange part of the appointment with her alone
B.why: Every woman should have at least one consultation without her partner or family present (CG110 1.1.14), and domestic abuse should be asked about when she is alone (NG201 1.2.5).

whyNot.0: His presence prevents a safe, private disclosure.
whyNot.1: Interpreters must be independent; a partner should not interpret (CG110 1.3.10).
whyNot.2: NICE says to ask at booking or the earliest opportunity when she is alone, not to delay.

B.q: During labour, a midwife in England sees physical signs that a 17-year-old has had FGM. What does the law require of the midwife?
options: Notify the police within one month of discovery
Seek the girl's consent before notifying anyone
Notify the police if the girl is under 16 years
Inform the GP in the discharge summary
B.why: FGM Act 2003 s5B: a regulated professional who sees signs of FGM in a girl under 18 must notify the police within one month. The notification does not breach confidence.

whyNot.1: The duty is mandatory; consent is not a precondition.
whyNot.2: The age limit is under 18, so a 17-year-old is covered.
whyNot.3: Telling the GP is good practice but does not discharge the police notification duty.

C.q: Amira, 33, discloses at 28 weeks that her partner is violent. She has a 3-year-old daughter at home and asks the midwife to tell nobody. She has capacity. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Respect her wishes, as she is an adult with capacity
Wait until she signs written consent to a referral
Share with children's social care and explain why
Note it in her hand-held notes and review next visit
C.why: A child in the home may be at risk. The safeguarding duty (Children Act 2004 s16LA) does not require consent and sharing does not breach confidence. CG110 1.1.9 says tell her why and when information is shared.

whyNot.0: Her capacity governs decisions about herself, not the protection of her daughter.
whyNot.1: Consent is not required to share information to safeguard a child.
whyNot.3: Hand-held notes may be read by the abuser, and delay leaves the child at risk.

C.q: A woman dies on the maternity unit from a postpartum haemorrhage. Later, a friend of hers phones the midwife asking what happened. Which statement about confidentiality is correct?
options: It ends once the death certificate is issued
It ends when the maternity episode is closed
It applies to the records but not to conversations
It continues after the woman has died
C.why: Code 5.3: respect that a person's right to privacy and confidentiality continues after they have died.

whyNot.0: Certification of death does not end the duty of confidentiality.
whyNot.1: Closing the episode is administrative; the duty continues.
whyNot.2: The duty covers all information about her, whether written or spoken.

C.q: A midwife on the labour ward is asked by a colleague from the antenatal clinic how her sister, who is in labour, is getting on. The colleague has no role in the sister's care. What should the midwife do?
options: Share brief details, as staff are bound by confidentiality
Decline, as the colleague is not involved in her care
Share the details if the colleague is a registered midwife
Look at the electronic record together with the colleague
C.why: Access is on a strict need-to-know basis (Caldicott principle 4). Being a colleague, or a relative, does not create a need to know.

whyNot.0: Staff confidentiality does not create a right to information about people not in their care.
whyNot.2: Registration status is not a reason to share; involvement in care is.
whyNot.3: Opening the record for someone not involved in care is an inappropriate access.

reteach.title: Her story, her choice, with one exception
reteach.question: Picture the woman holding a key to her information. Who can she hand it to, and when does the law open the door without her?

blocks.body: Door one: the care team, who see what they need for her care. Door two: everyone else, including partner, mother and friends, who see only what she chooses. Door three: safeguarding and public protection, opened without her key when a child or others are at risk. Even then, tell her why and when information is shared.

blocks.text: Next of kin has no automatic right to an adult woman's information. Consent, not relationship, opens door two.

explain.body: You owe confidentiality to everyone in your care. Respect privacy in all care (5.1), explain how information is used (5.2), remember it continues after death (5.3), share when safety overrides (5.4) and share with family as far as the law allows (5.5).

test.q: A midwife wants to show a student the notes of a woman she cared for last month, to illustrate a teaching point. The student had no role in her care. Which Code principle is most at stake?
options: Respecting her privacy and confidentiality
Keeping her records contemporaneous
Working within the limits of competence
Offering help in an emergency situation
test.why: Showing identifiable notes to someone not involved in care breaches privacy and confidentiality (Code 5). Teaching should use anonymised material.

whyNot.1: Contemporaneous records (Code 10) concern when entries are made, not who sees them.
whyNot.2: Competence (Code 13) is not the issue in sharing notes.
whyNot.3: Emergency help (Code 15) is unrelated to this situation.

explain.h: Partners and family on her terms
explain.body: Involve the partner according to the woman's wishes (NG194 1.1.3). See her alone at least once (CG110 1.1.14). Use an independent interpreter, not her partner, family or guardian (CG110 1.3.10).

test.q: Mei speaks little English. Her partner offers to interpret at booking. What should the midwife do?
options: Accept, as he knows her history well
Book a professional interpreter instead
Use a bilingual cleaner on the ward
Use the couple's 14-year-old son
test.why: CG110 1.3.10: provide an interpreter who is not a member of the woman's family, her legal guardian or her partner.

whyNot.0: A partner is not independent and may block disclosure of abuse.
whyNot.2: Untrained staff are not a professional interpreting service and confidentiality is compromised.
whyNot.3: Her son is a family member, whom CG110 1.3.10 excludes, and a child should not be asked to relay intimate maternity information.

explain.body: Share without consent when a child is at risk (Children Act 2004 s16LA: consent not required, no breach of confidence) or when FGM is found in a girl under 18 (police within one month, s5B). Share the minimum necessary and tell the woman why where it is safe.

children.label: Safeguarding assessment
children.sub: Risk to daughters or unborn girl

test.q: Grace, 24, has type 3 FGM identified at booking in England. She has a 4-year-old daughter. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Notify the police about Grace within one month
Record the FGM type and plan for deinfibulation
Assess the safeguarding risk to her daughter
Ask Grace to report it to the police herself
test.why: The s5B police duty applies to girls under 18. For an adult woman, assess the safeguarding risk to her daughter and any unborn girl.

whyNot.0: Grace is 24, so the mandatory police notification does not apply to her.
whyNot.1: Planning care in labour matters, but it does not address the risk to her daughter.
whyNot.3: Reporting is not her responsibility; the midwife must assess risk to the child.

explain.body: Hand-held notes hold a full record of care and test results (CG110 1.1.10) but abuse disclosures go in a confidential record (1.5.8). At transfer to health visitor or GP, share complications, mental health, FGM, safeguarding, parental responsibility and feeding (NG194 1.1.8).

test.q: Which information does NICE NG194 say should be shared when care transfers from the midwife to the health visitor?
options: Who has parental responsibility for the baby
The woman's attendance at antenatal classes
The birth partner's occupation and employer
The woman's preferred brand of nappies
test.why: NG194 1.1.8 includes who has parental responsibility for the baby, if known, alongside safeguarding, mental health, FGM and feeding.

whyNot.1: Antenatal class attendance is not on the NG194 1.1.8 transfer list.
whyNot.2: The partner's job is not clinical handover information.
whyNot.3: Nappy brand is a personal choice, not handover information.
